summary: FRONTIER: Beyond Earth is a first-person, browser-based mission game in which the player lands at the lunar south pole and must design, build and run Outpost Lantern using only what the site provides. Every decision is an engineering trade-off. Solar masts produce power in proportion to the sunlight their site receives, so placement on the ridge matters. Each module draws from a live power budget. Oxygen has to be made by electrolysing ice cored from a permanently shadowed crater where the suit loses heat. A regolith berm cuts the crew's radiation dose. Cargo capacity, suit oxygen and slope limits constrain every trip. Six milestones take the mission from touchdown to a self-sustaining base, and a base-management panel shows power, oxygen and dose in real time. A scanner and codex explain the real science behind each system, citing NASA LRO, LCROSS and ISS sources, and every fact is tagged Verified, Approximated or Fictional so students know what is real. The game runs on desktop and mobile with no install, in English, Russian and Spanish, and turns abstract mission trade-offs into choices players can feel.
details:
## What it does

FRONTIER: Beyond Earth is a first-person mission game that runs in any modern browser. The player lands on the Connecting Ridge at the lunar south pole and has to turn one lander into Outpost Lantern, a base that makes its own power and oxygen and shields its crew.

The mission runs through six milestones:

1. Touchdown: pulse the scanner to find deposits and scoop regolith.

2. First Light: raise solar masts on the ridge until they supply 3 kW.

3. Shelter: build a habitat, cover it with a regolith berm, and use the airlock.

4. Breath: find water ice in a permanently shadowed crater and build an oxygen electrolyzer.

5. Water in the Dark: build a lab, core the ice and run a spectrometer analysis.

6. Lantern: bring power, oxygen, shielding and science to green at the same time.

Every step is a trade-off the player has to manage. A mast's output is its 3 kW rating multiplied by the sunlight its site receives, so a few metres of height decide whether it works. Modules cannot be placed on slopes steeper than 8 degrees or out of cable range. Each module draws from a shared power budget, and the base sheds modules by priority if supply falls short. The electrolyzer burns stored ice to keep the oxygen balance positive. The berm cuts the daily radiation dose from 1.3 to 0.2 mSv. The suit has four minutes of oxygen, loses heat in shadow, and carries limited cargo, so every trip has to be planned. A base-management panel shows all of these numbers live.

## Benefits and intended impact

Students rarely get to run a whole mission from concept to operation, so trade-offs between power, mass, life support and site selection stay abstract. FRONTIER lets them make those decisions and see the consequences within about 15 to 30 minutes. A scanner and a ten-entry codex explain the real science behind each system, with sources from NASA's LRO, LCROSS and ISS programmes. Every fact and number is tagged Verified, Approximated or Fictional, so players learn what is known, what is estimated and what is game design. The game needs no install, account or payment, works on phones and low-end laptops, and is available in English, Russian and Spanish, which makes it usable in classrooms.

## Tools and technology

- TypeScript, three.js (WebGL2) and Vite

- Blender for the original low-poly models and textures, with a custom pipeline that packs models, converts textures to WebP and bakes the terrain and sunlight maps

- Web Audio API: all sound effects and music are synthesized in the browser, with no audio files

- Browser localStorage for saves; no server, keys or analytics

- Vercel for hosting

- NASA's Astronaut Glove 3D model for the first-person hand

- No special hardware; it runs on any device with a WebGL2 browser

## How it is creative

Most mission-design tools are menus and spreadsheets. FRONTIER puts the player on the surface, so engineering constraints are things they see and feel: the Sun sitting on the horizon, a hologram turning red on a steep slope, the suit cooling as they walk into a crater that has been dark for billions of years. The truth tags are our own idea for keeping a game honest about its science. The whole world, including audio, is generated or built by the team and loads as a small static site.

## What we considered

- Accuracy versus playability: lunar gravity, the low polar Sun, cold traps and electrolysis are real; rates and distances are tuned for a short session and labelled as approximations.

- Honesty about data: this alpha uses a procedural terrain shaped after the Connecting Ridge, not LOLA elevation data, and says so in-game. The pipeline is built to accept a LOLA crop next.

- Accessibility: touch controls, colour-blind modes, reduced motion, subtitles, a relaxed-oxygen option and adjustable HUD scale.

- Forgiving failure: running out of oxygen recalls the player to the last airlock save instead of ending the mission.

- Reach: a static site of about 12 MB with a low-quality tier for phones.
